title: Tale of the King of Hind and His Wazir

full_text:
In ancient India, King Vikram reigned over a vast empire of diverse peoples. When a province in the southern hills refused to pay taxes, the king’s military council urged an immediate invasion with war-elephants to burn the towns and subdue the rebels with fire and sword.

The King’s venerable vizier, Shimas, stepped forward and said: 'Sire, an empire is like an ancient banyan tree: if you cut down the branches because a few leaves are dry, you destroy the majesty of the whole. Let me visit the province alone, armed only with a staff and the scales of justice.'

The vizier rode to the southern hills.

He discovered that a severe drought had destroyed the rice harvest, and that the local governor had been extorting grain by force, driving the desperate peasants to rebellion.

Shimas dismissed the oppressive governor, opened the imperial emergency granaries to feed the starving families, and canceled all taxes for two years, distributing free seeds for the spring planting.

Moved to tears by his justice and mercy, the southern chiefs voluntarily laid down their weapons, pledged eternal loyalty to King Vikram, and sent fifty cartloads of fragrant spices to the capital as a token of gratitude!

King Vikram embraced his vizier, proclaiming: 'Your gentle justice has conquered a province that ten thousand war-elephants would have turned into a desert of ruins!'
moral: Gentle governance and equitable laws create lasting peace where iron force fails.
